title: Rebase onto main to keep history linear

scenario.brief:
Your `feature/csv` branch split from `main` a while ago, and `main` has since moved on (a teammate adjusted the tax rate). Before you open a pull request, you need your branch to sit on top of the latest `main`.

You have two options, and this is the decision the lab is about:

- **Merge `main` into your branch** — easy, but it adds a merge commit and tangles the history.
- **Rebase your branch onto `main`** — replays your commits on top of the latest `main`, keeping history **linear**.

Ledgerly's policy is a linear history on feature branches, so **rebase**. Your branch hasn't been shared, so rewriting it is safe.

**Approach.** On your feature branch, run `git rebase main`. Git replays your commits onto the current tip of `main`. The two changes touch different files, so there's nothing to resolve. When you're done, your branch should contain everything on `main` and still be a straight line — no merge commit.
scenario.whyItMatters: "Rebase or merge?" is a daily judgement call and a classic interview question. The mechanical difference is simple — rebase rewrites your commits onto a new base; merge records a join — but choosing the one that matches your team's history policy is what marks a fluent engineer.

objectives.title: Rebase your branch onto main, keeping history linear
objectives.description: feature/csv should contain main's latest commit, with no merge commit.
hints: Be on your feature branch (`git switch feature/csv`), then rebase onto the latest main.
`git rebase main` replays your commits on top of main. A `git merge main` instead would add a merge commit and fail the linear-history check.

debrief.summary: You rebased your feature branch onto the latest main, producing a clean linear history with your work replayed on top — the right choice under a linear-history policy.
internals: `git rebase main` found your branch's commits since it diverged, set your branch aside, moved to main's tip, and replayed each of your commits there as new commits (new ids).
The result is a straight line: main's history, then your commits — no merge commit joining two lines.
A `git merge main` would instead have created a two-parent merge commit, recording the divergence rather than erasing it. That fails the linear-history check here by design.
Rebase rewrites commits, so only do it on branches no one else has based work on.

keyCommands.note: Replay the current branch's commits on top of <base>.
The alternative: record a join with a merge commit.
See whether history is a straight line or has a merge.

commonMistakes: Merging main into the feature branch when the team wants a linear history.
Rebasing a branch others have already based work on — that rewrites shared commits.
Panicking at a conflict mid-rebase instead of resolving and running `git rebase --continue`.
debrief.atWork: Teams pick a convention — rebase for linear history, or merge to preserve the shape of integration. Knowing both, and which your repo expects, lets you keep a pull request clean and reviewable.
debrief.interview: "Rebase vs merge?" Answer: rebase replays commits onto a new base for a linear history (rewrites ids, local branches only); merge records a join with a merge commit (safe on shared branches). Choose by your team's history policy.
